text:
**For most people, LiFePO4 (LFP) is the better choice.** The sources I found mostly agree on this.

| | LiFePO4 | NMC |
|---|---|---|
| **Cycle life** | About 2,000-6,000 cycles | About 500-1,000 in most sources (one says up to 2,000) |
| **Failure behavior** | Milder: lower peak temperatures in lab tests | More violent: hotter, with flames in the tests |
| **Weight** | Somewhat heavier | Lighter at the cell level |
| **Price** | Median about $0.55/Wh in one catalog | About $0.95/Wh in the same catalog |
| **Availability** | Standard in nearly all current models | Mostly older or small units |

- **Cycle life is the biggest difference.** At one full cycle a day, a 500-cycle NMC unit lasts about 1.4 years, while a 3,000-cycle LiFePO4 unit lasts about 8 ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). Check the end point of a cycle rating. "To 70%" promises less than "to 80%" ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)).
- **Safety favors LFP, but it isn't fireproof.** In lab tests, LFP cells peaked at much lower temperatures when they failed. One study found that LFP reached thermal runaway sooner in an overcharge test. That makes it a milder failure, not an immune one ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/), [OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)).
- **NMC's weight advantage is smaller than you'd expect.** The cells are denser, but the case and inverter weigh the same either way. One database found only about a 10% gap per pound, and the Anker SOLIX C1000 (LFP) is lighter per Wh than the NMC Goal Zero Yeti 1000 ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/), [UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)).
- **Cold weather is a wash.** Both types generally won't charge below 32°F, and the limits depend more on the maker than the chemistry ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). One source claims NMC is worse in the cold, but others say it depends on the unit, so check the manual.

**When NMC makes sense:** a very light, compact unit that you'll use only a few times a year, or a heavily discounted unit you already know suits light use. If you already own a working NMC station, keep using it.

**An LFP example for home backup:** the [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2) is a 2,073.6 Wh LiFePO4 station with a 2,600 W inverter and a 6,000+ cycle rating. It carries a 5-year warranty and is not expandable. It lists at $899, and the listing says code AFF5OFF took it to $854.05 in BLUETTI's cart on 2026-10-24. Checkout has the final word on price. That link is an affiliate link, so the site earns a commission if you buy through it. Details are on the [listing page](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-elite-200-v2).

Whichever you pick, choose first by whether the output and capacity fit what you need to run, then by chemistry.
